title: Why the minority is kept (Mishnah Eduyot 1:5)
hook: minority opinions are recorded so a later court might rely on them

segments.voice: Yesterday, stories in the gaps: Cain's missing words, and several answers kept side by side. This week went from Rashi and Tosafot, to the Vilna page, two Talmuds, and the midrash of law and story. Today, why the losing side stays on the page. Day one thousand one hundred six.

A vote is taken. The motion passes. The sensible next step is to write down the result and move on. The people who voted no go home, and in a year nobody remembers what they argued. The Mishnah does something stranger. Page after page, it records the ruling and also the name of the person who disagreed, and what he said, and sometimes why. Rabbi so-and-so says otherwise. The sages say this. Why keep a losing argument at all? Why spend words on the side that lost? The Mishnah stops, in tractate Eduyot, to answer that very question about itself. Today's word is its answer.
screen: `THE MOTION PASSES.` → `THE NO VOTES ARE FORGOTTEN.` → `THE MISHNAH KEEPS THEM.`

segments.voice: Why the minority is kept. It's the Mishnah's own explanation, in Eduyot, of why it records a single opinion that lost. Start with the question as it asks it. The law follows the majority. So why mention the words of one person against the many? Second, its answer. So that if a later court sees that lone opinion and agrees with it, that court can rely on it. The minority view is kept on the shelf, not thrown away. A future court, in a different time, facing a different situation, might need exactly that view, and here it is, with a name attached. Third, the fine print, which is the clever part. The Mishnah adds that a court can't overturn the ruling of an earlier court unless it is greater than it, in wisdom and in number. That's a high bar. Some commentators put the two halves together: a minority opinion was part of the original discussion, so a later court can lean on it without having to overturn anyone. On that reading, the door was left open on purpose. Fourth, another voice, right next to it. The very next mishnah gives Rabbi Yehudah's reason, and it's different. The minority view is recorded so that if someone comes along and says, I have a tradition that says this, others can answer: you heard the opinion of that one sage, and the law didn't follow him. So one reason keeps the view alive, the other keeps it labeled. And the Mishnah, true to form, keeps both reasons. Why the minority is kept: the losing side might be needed, and it should be known for what it is.
screen: `THE LAW FOLLOWS THE MAJORITY.` · `A LATER COURT MIGHT RELY ON IT.` · `GREATER IN WISDOM AND IN NUMBER.` · `KEPT, AND LABELED.` · then, large: `THE MINORITY IS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is writing down a view you disagree with. If you have a pen or your phone, write one sentence: the strongest version of an opinion you don't hold. Not a straw version. The one its best defender would sign. Put a name next to it, if it belongs to someone. Then set it down and sit. Breathe. You don't have to agree with it. You're keeping it on the shelf, labeled, in case one day it's needed. Notice what it feels like to hold it carefully. The bell holds the time.
Why the minority is kept. The Mishnah's reason for recording losing opinions: a later court might rely on them, and they stay labeled as the minority. Today's word.
screen: `WHY THE MINORITY IS KEPT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the minority is kept. Today, when a decision goes your way at home or at work, write down the other side's best point anyway, with their name on it. Keep it. Day one thousand one hundred six.

howItsDone: Students of Mishnah and Talmud learn the minority opinions alongside the rulings, and later legal authorities sometimes cite a minority view when a situation calls for it.

fork.setup: you're editing the Mishnah. the law follows the majority, and one sage disagreed. what do you do with his words?
options: cut them; the law is settled.
keep them, with his name, in case a later court needs them.
rewrite them so he seems to agree.
fork.reveal: Eduyot keeps them, so a later court might rely on them, and, in Rabbi Yehudah's reason, so they stay labeled as the minority.

original.note: Hebrew: an individual. The Mishnah contrasts the words of the yachid with those of the many.

trapdoor: what you thought: losing opinions are kept out of politeness.
what it means: they are kept so a later court might rely on them, and so they're known as the minority.
what a scholar hears: Eduyot 1:5–6, the rule that a court overturns another only if greater in wisdom and in number, and Rabbi Yehudah's labeling reason.

notes: Week-end day (days 1100–1106): the review looks back briefly at the week.

Eduyot 1:5 and 1:6 are paraphrased. Please confirm: 1:5 (a later court may rely on the individual's view; a court can annul another's words only if greater in wisdom and in number) and 1:6 (Rabbi Yehudah: so that if someone claims a tradition, he can be told he heard the individual's view).

The teach says the later court can rely on the minority 'without overturning anyone'; this is a common explanation of 1:5 (e.g. Rabad / Rash on the mishnah) rather than the text's explicit words. Please confirm the framing.
Editor: the 'without overturning anyone' reading of 1:5 is now attributed in the voice to 'some commentators' rather than stated as the Mishnah's own words.
